title: The first words after
hook: he returns and says there is no Hindu and no Muslim, and the town asks what he means

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Bein, three days in the river, and a man who walked out changed. Today, the first thing he said.
screen: `THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER — SOME COME BACK CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The whole town has mourned him. They dragged the river. His sister wept. Then, on the third morning, he walks back into Sultanpur, alive, soaking wet, with a look on his face nobody can read. People crowd around. Where were you? What happened? Are you all right? The stories say he didn't answer. For a while he said nothing at all. He gave away what he owned and sat in silence. When he finally spoke, it wasn't an explanation. It was one short sentence, and it set the whole town talking.
screen: `THE TOWN HAD MOURNED HIM.` → `HE WALKS BACK IN, SILENT.` → `ONE SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence, as tradition remembers it: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. You met it on day six, as that day's line; this is where it comes from. Sultanpur had a Muslim governor, Hindu merchants and Muslim officials, temples and mosques, each community with its own rules about food, prayer and who you could marry. Who you were showed in your food, your prayers, your clothes. And the storekeeper back from the dead says: neither. What did he mean? The sources give no footnote, so Sikhs and scholars hear it in several ways. Some hear: before God, there are no labels. Beneath the Hindu and the Muslim are just people, all made by the one, Ik Onkar. Others hear a challenge: nobody around him was truly living up to what their faith asked, and he was calling both back to the heart of their own paths. And some hear the first sign of a new path, one defined by neither community. The readings don't cancel each other out; they can be held together. What the sentence clearly isn't is contempt. Nanak spent the rest of his life sitting with Hindus and Muslims, praying, singing, eating, arguing gently, and his companion on the road, Mardana, was a Muslim. Of course the town asked what he meant. And the town's religious judge, the qazi, decided to find out for himself.
screen: `THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.` · `A TOWN WHERE LABELS WERE EVERYTHING.` · `NO LABELS, A CHALLENGE, A NEW PATH.` · `NOT CONTEMPT.` · then, large: `BENEATH THE LABELS, PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one real person you usually see through a label: liberal, conservative, rich, poor, old, young, religious, not. Set the label down and look underneath, at someone who gets tired, who loves someone, who is afraid of something. Stay with that person, without the label, for a few slow breaths.
Sultanpur. The town where, back from the river, Nanak said: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.
Your line: beneath the labels, people. Tomorrow, the qazi asks him to pray. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's words after the river as the start of his mission, and often quote them as a teaching that all people are one before God.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: no one is Hindu, no one Muslim, the words tradition gives him.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nanak rejected both religions.
what it means: beneath the labels, people, all made by the one. and a call to live the heart of whatever path you're on.
what a scholar hears: the saying comes from the janamsakhis, not from a hymn. its setting in Sultanpur, under a Muslim governor with a mixed population, gives it its edge.

chat.says: What did Guru Nanak mean by 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim'?
options: People hear it several ways, like: beneath every label, we're all people made by the one.
He was mocking both communities and refused to spend time with either one.
He said it as a boy, arguing with his village teacher about the letters.
chat.meaning: He said it at Sultanpur, back from the river. Sikhs and scholars hear several readings, and none of them is contempt.

Sultanpur.meaning: the town where Nanak worked, and spoke after the river

Ik Onkar.meaning: the One, the first symbol of the Sikh scripture

Mardana.meaning: Nanak's Muslim companion, a musician who played the rebab

sources.ref: Janamsakhi traditions (Guru Nanak's words after the Bein: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim)
Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1 (the Sultanpur narrative)

notes: The saying is paraphrased/translated in the voice without a named translation (quoted: null). Macauliffe renders it (from memory) as 'There is no Hindu and no Musalman'; verify before quoting.
Gurmukhi of the saying (ਨਾ ਕੋ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨਾ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਨ) follows the common form 'na ko Hindu na Musalman'; confirm spelling.
Three readings are given without ranking; Keepers should confirm each is fairly described, especially 'the first sign of a new path', which some Sikhs stress and others downplay.
The period of silence and giving away possessions follows common tellings; confirm.
